reason: Stipules can be inconspicuous (small or hidden). The examples are correct. The one with 'obscured by pubescence' is a loose fit.
Tubercles are measured as length × width. The examples give widths.

Wrong reading. 'Carpels numerous' is a count (amount), and 'apical hairs absent' is about hairs, not carpels. 'Carpels not seen' is not a trait. Whether carpels are present is not a useful trait for a flora.
Nut fruits can be glabrous. The examples are correct.
PATO_0000001 (quality) is the root term and says nothing. The examples are other qualities (erect, recurved, glandular, glabrous), which belong under their own specific terms.
Clasping leaf bases are standard botany. The examples are correct. This assumes PATO_0104363 means 'clasping'. I did not look up its definition.
Ray flowers or rays can be slender. A rule should check that 'rays' means ray flowers and not umbel rays (branches). The examples are mixed.
Inflorescence branches and axes can be slender. The examples are correct.
The corolla lip is a flat lobe with an outline shape. Triangular is a valid shape. Some examples are about the apex or a middle lobe, which is a bearer-attribution issue, not a problem with the pair.
A perigynium (Carex) can be glabrous or hairy. The 'smooth' example is a different quality.

A pinna base can be 'oblique' in the sense of asymmetric, which is a shape. 'Oblique upward' or 'inclined' is an orientation. The pair is valid only for orientation. A rule would need to look at the word 'base' or at a following direction word.
A spathe can persist or fall off. 'Persistent' is the usual wording.
The epichile has a length. The examples are 'length × width' measurements.
Cupules are counted (1 or 2, 2–6). The examples are correct.
Peduncles can be winged, which is common in Asteraceae. The examples are correct.
Auriculate leaf bases are standard botany. The examples are correct.

'Divaricate-ascending' describes the angle or orientation of the pedicel, and 'fasciculate' describes how pedicels are grouped. Spatial pattern is too vague. A rule would map the angle words to orientation terms and the grouping words to the inflorescence.
A whole plant can be delicate or fragile. The examples are acceptable, though 'delicate' is a looser word than 'fragile'.
A spike has an outline shape (ovate, oblong, elliptic). The examples are correct.
'Wider than long' is a width-to-length ratio of the ligule. The examples are correct.
Perianth lobes can have an acute apex, which is a sharpness value. 'Spinose-tipped' is a different, more specific quality.
Sepal margins can be erose. The examples are correct.
Leaflets can be velutinous. The examples are correct.

'Unequal' compares lobes with each other, and 'reduced to mucros' is a different statement. Size is valid for a single lobe's size. A rule would need to send 'unequal' to a relational term and keep only absolute size words here.
A root (especially a taproot) can be filiform. The examples are correct.
A seta can be erect. The examples are correct.

Ray flowers (ligules) can be scabrous or papillose. However, the examples ('main branches smooth proximally', 'near nodes') are about stems or branches, so 'ray' is read wrongly. A rule would need to tell ray flowers from rays (branches).
Stem nodes are often pubescent, and the examples are correct.
An indusium (fern) can bear hairs or glands. The examples are correct.
The summit or mouth of a leaf sheath can be concave (sedges). The examples are correct.
A leaf sheath can be thin. The examples are correct.
Floral bracts have a colour. The examples are correct.
An ovary can be twisted (orchids, ovary and pedicel). The examples are correct.
A stalk (stipe) can be red-brown or chestnut-brown. The examples are correct.
The epichile has a width. The examples are width or 'length × width' measurements.
Leaf lobes have a colour. The 'stellate pubescent' example is a hair trait, not a colour.
Pedicels can be elongate. The examples are correct, though one is about peduncles.
Achene surfaces can be rugulose. The examples are correct.
The rostellum has a length in mm. The examples are correct.
Nut fruits can be glabrous or have hairs of different kinds. The examples are correct.
A lamina can be pointed at the apex or base. The examples are correct, though they really describe the apex or base, not the whole lamina.
Inflorescence axes can be pubescent. The examples are correct.
Secondary veins can be pubescent. The examples are correct.
A lamina can be flat, or flattened in the sense of folded or channelled versus flat. The examples are correct.
A corolla (mouth) can be oblique. The examples are correct.
Stigma lobes can be spreading. The examples are correct.
An ovary can be trilobate (three-lobed). The examples are correct.
Pedicels can be swollen. The examples are correct, although several are about the articulation, which is only part of the pedicel.
A leaflet lamina has hair types. The examples are correct.
Inflorescence branches can be spreading. The examples are correct.
A capitulum can be nodding. The examples are correct.
A branch can be prostrate. The examples are correct.
A leaf can be glaucous. The examples are correct, though some are about the sheath, which is part of the leaf.
The apex of a leaf sheath can be truncate. The examples are correct.
A hypanthium can be hemispheric. The examples are correct.
An ovary apex can be truncate. The examples are correct.
Wrong reading. In PATO, 'condensed' (synonym 'compressed') means packed or squashed together. For 'laterally compressed' sheaths the right term is 'flattened' (PATO_0002254).
Calyx lobes can be oblong. The examples are correct.
A perigynium can be punctate or puncticulate (dotted, with glands or resin). The examples all come from one flora, with some garbled text.
PATO_0000001 (quality) is the root term and says nothing. The examples are other qualities (glabrous, ciliate, grooved, flattened), which belong under their own specific terms.
